title: E155 Portfolio
text:
In this lab, we made an encoder to measure and calculate the revolutions per minute a motor goes. This was successful and we know the motor doesn’t skip any pulses based on the fact that if it would miss a pulse it would mess up the readings really bad (switch in direction).
Spent a total of 17 hours





Electrical Schematic


Note, polarity and voltage of power supply is not specified, this affects RPS and dierction






Lab5 Flowchart





For the 1Hz refreshing of data, we used the 1ms Timer 2 clock and made it create an interrupt whenever it overflowed with an ARR value of 999, meaning that the frequency we would get from this would be:
(999+1 pulses) / (1000 pulses/s) = 1second
This is good also because it is asynchronous and will not lag with the Exernal Interrupts.
The motor has 408 pulses per revolution, which if we have 2 channels and a rising and falling edge, this means we get 408*4 = 1632 counts per revolution.
to calculate RPS, we do:
Counts / (4x408x(999+1)/(1000)), where Counts is the amount of rising and falling edges in both PA1 and PA2. 408*4 is the counts per revolution, and (999+1)/(1000) is the duration of the timer
if we get 1632 counts in 1 second, we get: 1632 / (4x408x(999+1)/(1000)) = 1 rps, which is expected
When reading at around 12v, we read a RPS value of around 2.7, which is close to the rated 150RPM (2.5RPS), which could also be a bit higher since we don’t have a load on the motor.
Another test done is that when the voltage is set at a value that will make the RPS we read to be around 1 (closer to 1.007) we counted for 60 steps while having a timer and read a time of 58.90 seconds, which is 60/58.9 = 1.02rps, which is very close to 1.007






Pulling Example


In this code, you can see how it is set up to count how many times it could read a value in a pin per second, but this has a lot of issues. First, we are reading and waiting to read when we get a pulse, which means that we are either at the right point in time, or have to wait and delay. In this example, it sampled around 30k times per second, but this while loop was only ~4 lines of code on average, this means that if we add more sensors or interrupts, the sampling frequency will both drop and be inconsistent, not also considering that we can’t fully sample the function if it is above half the sampling frequency, which would also drop if we add more pins to read or a more complicated code.



Interrupt Microcontroller output





Interrupt Example


Interrupts allow us to skip all of this and only run the code when we read something, saving processing power and making the reaction time more “continuous” instead of fitting at a specific discrete point in time.
In this example, the fastest frequency it was able to read was around 45k, but it also looked like the higher the frequency, the slower it printed values, where at 50k, it would not be able to print an output. This is probably because it has so many interrupts it can’t run the print statement code. 50k is much more than the maximum theoretical of 16k the pooling can achieve, and note that this has more precision where in the pooling case, measuring something like 15.9kHz may need hundreds of cycles to differenciate from 16kHz (because it is close to sampling rate), but with interrupts it is very precise at all values under 45k.






AI Prototype


Based on this code, we can see how a step is defined if a and b are not equal, or when they are equal it makes it in the opposite direction. this is either not checking both the rising and falling edge, or plain wrong since if we follow the pattern of 00, 01, 11, 10 … the pattern would go back and forth, adding 1 in the 00 and 11, subtracting in 01 and 10. This may work since it uses two different interrupts similar to ours, but it differs that it reads the pulses inside the interrupt. I wanted to avoid doing this to make the interrupts run as fast as possible.



Lab 5 code: https://github.com/cojedadesilva/E155_Labcode_CODS/tree/main/lab5

title: E155 Portfolio
text:
In this lab, we were tasked to make a display for a 4x4 keyboard that would show a different hex number after pressing a button, saving two numbers at a time.
This Lab took around 18 hours to finish.


In the Lab1, we used 5v as the V_in of the 7 segment display, which makes the display bleed a bit of current into every LED when off since 3.3v < 5v. This was fixed by changing the V_in to 3.3v and recalculating the required resistance to be:
For these LED’s, we used a 160Ω resistor
Voltage drop of around 0.4V in the transistor, a red LED has a voltage drop of around 1.8v at the current we are driving them at, so:
\[
0.010 > \frac{3.3-0.4-1.8}{R}
\] \[
R > 110
\]
For the transisitor, we need to calculate the resistor that we will connect to the base: The desired base current is between 2-3 mA based on the datasheet and our desired output current (up to 70mA) and the voltage drop would be around 0.95Vm, we need to account that the total voltage is 3.3v, so:
\[
R = \frac{3.3-0.95}{0.005}
\] \[
R = 470
\]
In this case, we also chose 10mA for the 7 segment display since the datasheet does recommend a value closer to that, and it was very visible. The selected value was 160Ω. This value was also used for the normal LED’s used in the fulladder since they have similar current needs and voltage drops.
This also corresponds to teh current ratings of teh 2N3906 Transistor we are using, which allows a maximum of 200mA to be drawn, meaning that having all segments on (7 per transistor) results in a total current draw of <70mA.






Block Diagram








Circuit Diagram





The current code made works in an interesting way. We first defined a top module that is in charge of getting the clock and sending the calculated sout (data on specific hex number to display at a given time) to the sevseg module that controls the seven segment display. The oter module it calls is leds_co, which is in charge of managing all the seven segment LED logic, where we have to flip back and forth to only use 9 pins instead of 14 (more on this in lab2 website).
In this case, we need to drive the rows at different times and read the columns, to prevent bouncing in the buttons and drive power to rows, we used the counter, specifically the range [25:23] and [21], where the 21’st bit will save col -> savecol on the rising edge. In order to control the row output, we use the range [25:24], where we use the left shift operator to make the sequence, were this value can be anything from 0 to 3.
1 << 0 = 0001
1 << 1 = 0010
1 << 2 = 0100
1 << 3 = 1000
Then it repeats
The 23’rd bit is used in the keypad decoder code where we only act on the rising edge of this bit since this is halfway from a row being assigned and it being unasigned, meaning any start behaviour and end behavior noise we get should not fall in the middle. generally this can be done by adding counters that check the signal a specific time after the row is switched (less robust), or other methods to reduce this noise may include low pass filters (not ideal for digital electronics since voltage in capacitors takes time to rise) or reducing frequency to reduce the percent of time where you have noise (ideally avoided to reduce unnecesary noise)
The debouncer logic (shown below) works in a simple manner, where we start in the ~pressed state, this means we aren’t actively pressing the button. when something gets detected, col would not be 0, which is when we set N2 = N1 and N1 = {counter[2:1],coln}, where:
counter[2:1] is the same part of the counter that controls row. Note that this variable inside the keydec module is different from the 32 bit counter. coln is defined as the column number, were we use if statements to the opposite to when we assigned rows:
0001 –> 0
001x –> 1
01xx –> 2
1xxx –> 3
In the code, it was chosen to use if statements instead of assuming that x were 0 since if you would press 3 buttons at once and release the first one that was detected, it could default to the first column, which is unpredictable behaviour we like to avoid.






FSM of the debouncer





FSM transition diagram


Note: the FSM changes states on the rising edge of counter[23], not the clock directly.






Testbench of the Counter





Testbench of the keyboard decoder





Testbench of the ledlogic module





Testbench of the top module





Did the All at once:



Testbench of the top module


The AI gave me all the modules at once, but it looks like it ran out of space and gave me a partial top module as seen as the upper error.
After asking the AI to redo teh top module, it got confused of the other module names and got more errors. I have to either probably use option B to try get each module individually, or buy premium AI use (used free access)
Using option B, we get:



Testbench of the top module


which basically means that the AI messed up some basic syntax. This is probably a quick fix that the AI would be able to fix if we input the errors and it will give us a nicer output.
Overall, I noticed with both of these solutions that the AI response was way longer than my code, which could mean the AI actually knows how to code, or it is overseeing a lot of easy ways to make a verilog code more compact.



Verilog Code: https://github.com/cojedadesilva/E155_Labcode_CODS/tree/main/lab3
Lab2 Code: https://github.com/cojedadesilva/E155_Labcode_CODS/tree/main/lab2
HDSP-521A datasheet: https://docs.broadcom.com/doc/HDSP-521A-523A-Dual-Digit-General-Purpose-7-Segment-Display-DS
Transistor datasheet: https://www.onsemi.com/pdf/datasheet/2n3906-d.pdf

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
During this lab, we are tasked to make a 2.4Hz square wave, an and gate operation, a xor gate operation and a translator from binary introduced from switches into a hex number in a 7 segment display. These different tasks explore different types of skill when working with FPGA’s.
This Lab took around 12 hours to finish.

PCB soldering and circuits
First, we have to make sure the FPGA setup will be adecuate for the E155 course, where we need to include all the components and verify the connections and board all work propperly. This helped me develop skills mainly in surface mounted devices, since it is a type of soldering I am not very familiar.



Board after Soldering


After getting the board set up, we started to work into making the circuit for the following parts of the lab. This required some amount of calculations and design choices that are gone more in depth later in this page.



Block Diagram





Circuit Diagram


It is also important to note that we had to program which pins are which in the FPGA setup:



FPGA pin setup




and/xor gate operations
This can be easily done in verilog by defining the output (an LED in this case) to be the “and” or “xor” operation of the desired inputs. This can be done as easily as:
assign led00 = s[0] ^ s[1]; //xor
assign led10 = s[2] & s[3]; //and


2.4 Hz Timing
In order to get a frequency as close as possible to 2.4Hz, we need to make a counter that resets 2.4 times per second, this can be achieved by making a large register counter (32 bits in my case) and considering that we have a clock speed of 48MHz and a desired frequency of 2.4Hz, we can do the following math:
\[
2.4 = \frac{f*c}{2^(N-1)}
\] Where \[
N = 32
\] \[
f = 48,000,000
\] \[
c = 215
\]
The value 215 was chosen to give us the closest frequency to the desired 2.4 Hz. This would result in a code that looks like this:
    always_ff @(posedge int_osc)
        begin
            counter <= counter + 215; //107 * 48,000,000 ~= 2.4 * 2^30, so a 2.4Hz square wave
        end
  assign fpga_blink_out = counter[31];
After getting this code working, we tested the signal generated using an oscilloscope and verified it was at 2.4Hz.



Oscilloscope trace




7 segment display
To make the 7 segment display to work by being controlled by the UPduino board, we first need to consider that the 7 segment display we are using (HSDP-511A) works by grounding the pins to turn on the desired segment. This means that whenever we are making the logic on which segments turn on and off, we have to consider that 0 is on and 1 is off. This was made in System Verilog and tested using a testbench, where we made a test case for each of the possible combinations of 4 switches (16 tests).



Top Testbench Trace





LED Logic Testbench Trace





Seven Segment Testbench Trace


Haiving the error vector always in 0’s tells us that the testbench was successful. This better confirms that we will get a working FPGA programming.
The next thing to decide was the resistance added to each pin. Adding an individual resistor per pin allows us to have a consistent brightness in every segment and segment combination. This resistance value was chosen to make current through each segment under 5mA, which is not even close to the maximum recomended, but it should extend its working life. This was done assuming a voltage drop of 2.1 volts as seen in the datasheet to be:
\[
0.005 > \frac{5-2.1}{R}
\] \[
R > 580
\]
In this case, we chose to use 1k resistors since they were visible and available.



Test with 9 in binary (1001) showing the right output


From this expected output image, we can see how the XOR LED is on and the AND led is off. This is expected since both modules work at the same time.


AI Prototype
Using ChatGPT, we inputted the folowing prompt:
Write SystemVerilog HDL to leverage the internal high speed oscillator in the Lattice UP5K FPGA and blink an LED at 2 Hz. Take full advantage of SystemVerilog syntax, for example, using logic instead of wire and reg.
from which we got this code:
module led_blinker_2hz (
    output logic led
);

    // High-speed internal oscillator output
    logic clk_48mhz;

    // Instantiate the HFOSC (internal high-frequency oscillator)
    SB_HFOSC #(
        .CLKHF_DIV("0b00") // Divide by 1 → 48 MHz
    ) hfosc_inst (
        .CLKHFEN(1'b1),    // Enable the HF oscillator
        .CLKHFPU(1'b1),    // Power up the oscillator
        .CLKHF(clk_48mhz)
    );

    // Parameters for 2 Hz blinking (toggle every 0.5s)
    localparam int unsigned MAX_COUNT = 24_000_000 - 1;

    // Counter and LED register
    logic [24:0] counter = 0;

    always_ff @(posedge clk_48mhz) begin
        if (counter == MAX_COUNT) begin
            counter <= 0;
            led <= ~led;  // Toggle the LED
        end else begin
            counter <= counter + 1;
        end
    end

endmodule
After testing this code, we realized that it didn’t work, we copied the error message and tried the new code.
module led_blinker_2hz (
    output logic led
);

    logic clk;

    // Instantiate the OSC block
    osc_0 osc_inst (
        .clkout(clk)
        // Add enable or other ports if necessary
    );

    // Blink at 2 Hz (assuming 48 MHz oscillator)
    localparam int unsigned MAX_COUNT = 24_000_000 - 1;
    logic [24:0] counter = 0;

    always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
        if (counter == MAX_COUNT) begin
            counter <= 0;
            led <= ~led;
        end else begin
            counter <= counter + 1;
        end
    end

endmodule
After running this, it would still not work, This could be that mainly the system we are using and the way libraries have to be called are extremely specific and difficult for a general LLM model like ChatGPT to do without messing up.
If I would continue trying to fix the errors with chat and think about possible promts I could add to induce debugging, it is defenitely possible to get a working code.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display
text:
In this Lab, we were tasked to make 2 HEX displays using a single module by multiplexing, and showing the addition of both HEX numbers in a 5 bit binary LED display. This lab uses a code almost identical to last lab, with a few changes. This resulted in a succesful lab2 where we were able to get the two hex numbers displayed with minimal use of pins and showing the sum on LED’s.
This lab took around 10 hours to complete.

Circuits and Diagrams
First, we start by making a circuit that can support using two multiplexed 7 segment displays, thsi was done by controlling the power input of each display with a PNP transistor and outputting the 7 segment signal to the current display we are powering.



Electrical schematic of teh Lab 2 circuits


This looks like this after assembly:



Lab 2 wiring


After wiring the circuit like this, it was configured as follows to be able to control it using verilog code:



FPGA pin setup


This was then used in our top module, which uses code that was made in Lab1 (lab1_co.sv, which controls the 7 segment display) and the code that controls all the logic and switching between displays.
/*
by Carlos Ojeda de Silva, September 10 2025
cojedadesilva@g.hmc.edu
This file combines both tasks for lab2
*/
module top(
    input   logic [3:0] s1, s2,
    output  logic [1:0] disps,
    output  logic [6:0] number,
    output  logic [4:0] leds
);
logic [3:0] sout;
leds_co leds_co(s1[3:0], s2[3:0], disps, sout[3:0], leds[4:0]);
sevseg sevseg(sout[3:0], number[6:0]);
endmodule
This top module results in a block diagram that looks as follows:



Top module Block Diagram



Curcuit calculations:
In the previous lab, we used 5v as the V_in of the 7 segment display, which makes the display bleed a bit of current into every LED when off since 3.3v < 5v. This was fixed by changing the V_in to 3.3v and recalculating the required resistance to be:
Math for the yellow LED’s for the 5bit display, in this case, the FPGA is not recommended to use over 8mA and the yellow LED has a 2v drop, so:
\[
0.008 > \frac{3.3-2}{R}
\] \[
R > 130
\]
For these LED’s, we used a 160Ω resistor
Voltage drop of around 0.4V in the transistor, a red LED has a voltage drop of around 1.8v at the current we are driving them at, so:
\[
0.010 > \frac{3.3-0.4-1.8}{R}
\] \[
R > 110
\]
For the transisitor, we need to calculate the resistor that we will connect to the base: The desired base current is between 2-3 mA based on the datasheet and our desired output current (up to 70mA) and the voltage drop would be around 0.95V:
\[
R = \frac{0.95}{0.0025}
\] \[
R = 380
\]
In this case, we also chose 10mA for the 7 segment display since the datasheet does recommend a value closer to that, and it was very visible. The selected value was 160Ω. This value was also used for the normal LED’s used in the fulladder since they have similar current needs and voltage drops.
This also corresponds to teh current ratings of teh 2N3906 Transistor we are using, which allows a maximum of 200mA to be drawn, meaning that having all segments on (7 per transistor) results in a total current draw of <70mA.



7 Segment Display Multiplexing
For this part of the lab, we first need to use the 7 segment display code from Lab1, where all we have to chnage is the input and how the output is treated. To do this we first connected both PNP transistor’s power (Emmiter) to the 3.3v line. Then we connected the Base to the FPGA pins so whenever they are high, the transistor switches. Finally we connected each 7 segment display power to the collector. We also added a pulldown resistor (chose 10k since it is standard and much larger than the 160Ω chosen for the display) to the PNP transistor to remove any excess charge accumulated when switching off. Here is the verilog code used:
/*
by Carlos Ojeda de Silva, September 10 2025
cojedadesilva@g.hmc.edu
This file controls which 7 segment display is used with the corresponding s values. It also outputs the sum of 2 numbers in binary with 5 leds
*/
module leds_co(
    input logic [3:0] s1, s2,
    output  logic [1:0] disps,
    output logic [3:0] sout,
    output logic [4:0] leds
);

    logic int_osc;
    logic pulse; 
    logic led_state = 0;
    logic [31:0] counter = 0;
    
    // Internal high-speed oscillator 
    HSOSC hf_osc (.CLKHFPU(1'b1), .CLKHFEN(1'b1), .CLKHF(int_osc));
    
    // Simple clock divider
    
    always_ff @(posedge int_osc)
        begin
            counter <= counter + 215; //this value works
            if (counter[21]) sout = s1;
            if (~counter[21]) sout = s2; //using index 21 makes it around 2.5kHz, which is higher than human eye and slow enough for the transistor.
            leds = s1 + s2;
        end
  assign disps[0] = counter[21];
  assign disps[1] = ~counter[21];
endmodule
This code was mainly recycled from the lab1 code also named leds_co.sv, where the logic was changed to select the display with the disps variable. The same addition was chosen as the previous lab, but since 2.4Hz is too slow, we reduced the exponent from 31 to 21 to make it 1048 (2^10) times faster, resulting in 2.5kHz. This is much faster than the human eye being at at most in the hundreds of Hz.


5 Bit Full Adder
To make the full adder, we first need to consider we are adding two 4-bit numbers, meaning that the sum could be 5 bits long, meaning that our output will be of length 5. Then we used the following line of verilog code to assign the leds the sum:
  assign leds = s1+s2;
Finally, the pins are assigned so the LED’s order matches one that can be interpreted from left to right.


Testbench
To test the fpga setup, we have designed a testbench that tests every hex value for each display (0-15 display 1 then stays at 15 while the second one goes from 0-15).
The test bench was also made by doing small modifications to the code, where we can control the timing (counter[21]) to force it to switch between displays.



Top Testbench Trace





Seven Segment Testbench Trace





Multiplexing/LED logic Testbench Trace


This test bench showed that the system works for any of these inputs, but there are a total of 16x16x2 = 512 possible inputs, so take into consideration that some real world testing may be needed to verify it always works, or expand the testbench.


AI Prototype
Using ChatGPT, we inputted the folowing prompt:
Write SystemVerilog HDL to time multiplex a single seven segment decoder (that decodes from four bits to a common anode seven segment display) to decode two sets of input bits and drive two sets of seven output bits.
from which we got this code:
module seven_segment_mux (
    input logic clk,               // Clock input to drive time multiplexing
    input logic rst_n,             // Active low reset
    input logic [3:0] digit1,      // First 4-bit input digit (for first 7-segment display)
    input logic [3:0] digit2,      // Second 4-bit input digit (for second 7-segment display)
    output logic [6:0] seg1,       // 7-segment display 1 output (active low)
    output logic [6:0] seg2        // 7-segment display 2 output (active low)
);

    // Internal signals
    logic [3:0] current_digit;
    logic [1:0] display_selector;  // 2-bit selector to multiplex between display 1 and display 2

    // 7-segment decoder for common anode display
    function [6:0] seg_decoder(input logic [3:0] digit);
        case (digit)
            4'b0000: seg_decoder = 7'b1111110; // 0
            4'b0001: seg_decoder = 7'b0110000; // 1
            4'b0010: seg_decoder = 7'b1101101; // 2
            4'b0011: seg_decoder = 7'b1111001; // 3
            4'b0100: seg_decoder = 7'b0110011; // 4
            4'b0101: seg_decoder = 7'b1011011; // 5
            4'b0110: seg_decoder = 7'b1011111; // 6
            4'b0111: seg_decoder = 7'b1110000; // 7
            4'b1000: seg_decoder = 7'b1111111; // 8
            4'b1001: seg_decoder = 7'b1111011; // 9
            default: seg_decoder = 7'b0000000; // Blank (invalid input)
        endcase
    endfunction

    // Time multiplexing logic
    always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (~rst_n) begin
            display_selector <= 2'b00; // Start with first display
        end else begin
            // Toggle the display selector every clock cycle
            display_selector <= display_selector + 1;
        end
    end

    // Output logic: Multiplex between two sets of 7-segment displays
    always_comb begin
        case (display_selector)
            2'b00: begin
                current_digit = digit1;    // Drive the first 7-segment display
                seg1 = seg_decoder(current_digit);
                seg2 = 7'b1111111; // Turn off second display
            end
            2'b01: begin
                current_digit = digit2;    // Drive the second 7-segment display
                seg1 = 7'b1111111; // Turn off first display
                seg2 = seg_decoder(current_digit);
            end
            2'b10: begin
                current_digit = digit1;    // Drive the first 7-segment display
                seg1 = seg_decoder(current_digit);
                seg2 = 7'b1111111; // Turn off second display
            end
            2'b11: begin
                current_digit = digit2;    // Drive the second 7-segment display
                seg1 = 7'b1111111; // Turn off first display
                seg2 = seg_decoder(current_digit);
            end
            default: begin
                seg1 = 7'b1111111;
                seg2 = 7'b1111111;
            end
        endcase
    end

endmodule

This code actually compiled, but it looks a bit off: -only goes from 0-9 it was never specified that it had to be hex to be fair. -only does low=high logic for the case(display_selector) but not for the seg_decoder, thsi can be fixed with a simple “~”. -It wasnts us to use 7 segment outputs, so instead of switching with the transistor by turnig power on and off, it turns the pins on and off. using more pins than needed.
but I still think it was a high quality output since it did make something that compiled and has around 70% of the logic right, while only taking 2 min to make and test.
The only part of the code that looks different to what I usually make is the use of a function. I imagined you always made a new module, but I think I can use it for Lab3 to make a demultiplexer.
I believe if we dumb down the specifics (7 pins for display and 2 for power that switch back and forth) it would work well

title: E155 Portfolio
text:
In this lab, we made a melody player code for a STM32L4 microcontroller where we can control the frequency and timing of musical notes.
This lab took 24 hours





Electrical Schematic





We chose TIM2 because it has 32 bits and it is easy to change frequency by alering the ARR and SRC values
Minimum frequency
Since our PSC is 39, and ARR is a 32 bit number, the maximum value it could have is, the maximum possible frequency (tested) is when ARR is 1, or: 4,000,000/((39+1)(2^32))/2 = 1.164x10^-5 Hz, we divide by 2 because we toggle every cycle.
Maximum frequency
Since our PSC is 39, the maximum possible frequency (tested) is when ARR is 1, or: 4,000,000/((39+1)(1+1))/2 = 25kHz, we divide by 2 because we toggle every cycle.
Minimum delay
since our maximum frequency is 25kHz, the minimum delay we can do is 1/(2*25,000) or 0.2ms
Maximum delay
since our minimum frequency is 1.164x10^-5 Hz, we get: 1/(2*1.164x10^-5) = 42950s or 11:55:50 hours (11.93)
Frequency within 1%
Worst case escenario we get an ARR that is at most 0.5 off, so: \[
ARR = \frac{2,000,000}{40*f_d} - 1
\] And therefore: \[
f_d = \frac{2,000,000}{40*(ARR+1)}
\] We then calculate the worst case escenario frequency change when changing ARR by 0.5 (it will get rounded, so it can be at most off by 0.5) \[
\frac{df}{dARR} = \frac{-2,000,000}{40*(ARR+1)^2}
\] now, we can calculate the percent error by multiplying by 0.5 and dividing by desired frequency: \[
error = \frac{-2,000,000}{40*f_d*(ARR+1)^2} = \frac{1}{2(ARR+1)}
\] for 1% error, the maximum ARR accepted is: \[
0.01 >= \frac{1}{2(ARR+1)}
\] ARR >= 49
ARR of 49 corresponds to a frequency of: \[
f_d = \frac{2,000,000}{40*(49+1)} = 1000 Hz
\]
And since we can get way larger ARR values, the clock does tick within 1% of the frequency in all frequencies between 220 and 1000 Hz



After asking ChatGPT, we got the following response:



AI Prototype


This is similar to what we concluded, where we chose Timer 2 since it seemed easier to use and has the ability to count up to 32 bits, which since we were originally considering using timer overflow to control notes instead of number of clock cycles we used in the end. this also made me understand better the math behind it.

Audio Amplifier https://www.ti.com/lit/ds/symlink/lm386.pdf
Math in Desmos: https://www.desmos.com/calculator/p6powqxlh8
